o: Rinse the mouth after each inhalation and use a spacer

q: During an acute gout flare, colchicine relieves pain chiefly by?

A 34-year-old woman presents with anemia, a platelet count of 25,000/mm³, and prolonged PT and APTT. A peripheral blood smear image is provided. Based on these findings, which fusion gene is most likely involved?
ex: PML-RARA The clinical presentation of pancytopenia, coagulopathy (raised PT/APTT, suggesting DIC), and the key morphological finding of a promyelocyte with multiple Auer rods (a faggot cell) on the peripheral smear are pathognomonic for Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL), a subtype of AML. APL is cytogenetically characterized by a specific translocation between chromosome 15 and 17, denoted as t(15;17)(q24;q21). This translocation creates a fusion gene between the Promyelocytic Leukemia (PML) gene on chromosome 15 and the Retinoic Acid Receptor Alpha (RARA) gene on chromosome 17. The resulting PML-RARA fusion protein acts as a transcriptional repressor, blocking the differentiation of myeloid cells at the promyelocyte stage. This is the molecular hallmark of APL. The other fusion genes are associated with different subtypes of AML : RUNX1-RUNX1T1 with t(8;21) and INV 16 with inv(16).

q: Which gene is most commonly implicated in the carcinoma stage depicted in the image shown?
ex: BRAF V600E The image displays the classic histological features of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC), which is the most common type of thyroid cancer. The most common genetic alteration found in PTC is a point mutation in the BRAF gene, specifically the V600E mutation. This mutation occurs in approximately 45-50% of all PTC cases and is a driver mutation that leads to constitutive activation of the MAP kinase signaling pathway, promoting cell proliferation and survival. The BRAF V600E mutation is particularly associated with the classic and tall cell variants of PTC and is often linked to more aggressive tumor behavior and a higher risk of recurrence. RET/PTC rearrangements (Option B) are also common in PTC, especially in radiation-associated cases. RAS mutations (Option A) are more characteristic of Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma. P53 mutations (Option D) are associated with poorly differentiated and Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma.

The clinical symptoms fit well with this diagnosis. The tingling sensation in the legs can be due to peripheral neuropathy caused by the monoclonal protein or amyloid deposition. q: The immunohistochemical marker TTF- 1 (thyroid transcription factor-1) is most commonly expressed in which of the following tumors or tissues?
ex: Lung adenocarcinoma Thyroid Transcription Factor-1 (TTF-1), also known as NKX2-1, is a nuclear transcription factor that plays a crucial role in the development of the thyroid, lung, and forebrain. In pathology, TTF-1 is used as an immunohistochemical (IHC) marker to determine the origin of tumors. It shows strong nuclear staining in the vast majority of lung adenocarcinomas (around 75-85%) and small cell lung carcinomas. It is also positive in all types of well-differentiated thyroid carcinomas, including papillary (Option C) and follicular types. However, when differentiating metastatic tumors of unknown primary, a positive TTF-1 stain is most commonly indicative of a lung or thyroid origin. Between the options of lung adenocarcinoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma, it is a key marker for both. In the context of lung cancer differentiation, it is the primary marker for adenocarcinoma. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung (Option A) is typically TTF-1 negative.

q: A patient is found to have a cerebellar mass along with a renal tumor and reports a family history of similar illnesses. Which genetic mutation is most likely present in this family?
ex: VHL The triad of a cerebellar mass (specifically a hemangioblastoma), a renal tumor (specifically clear cell renal cell carcinoma), and a positive family history is the classic presentation of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. VHL is an autosomal dominant hereditary cancer syndrome caused by a germline mutation in the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3. This mutation predisposes individuals to the development of various benign and malignant tumors. In addition to cerebellar hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinomas, patients with VHL disease are also at risk for retinal angiomas, pheochromocytomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. The other options are different hereditary cancer syndromes : Neurofibromatosis (NF) involves neurofibromas and optic gliomas, Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC) involves hamartomas in multiple organs, and Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53 mutation) is associated with sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenal cortical carcinoma.

q: A 30-year-old football player is brought to the emergency department after a sudden collapse due to cardiac arrest. A histological image is provided. Based on the microscopic findings shown, what is the most likely cause of death?
ex: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) Sudden cardiac death in a young athlete is most commonly caused by an underlying, often undiagnosed, cardiac condition. The histological image shows the pathognomonic features of Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM), which include cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, extensive myofiber disarray (where the muscle cells are arranged in a chaotic, whorled pattern instead of being parallel), and interstitial fibrosis. HCM is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins, leading to unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy. This hypertrophy and disarray create a substrate for fatal ventricular arrhythmias (like ventricular fibrillation), which are the usual cause of sudden death, especially during or after intense physical exertion. The other cardiomyopathies have different histological features : DCM (Option B) shows thinned walls and attenuated fibers, RCM (Option C) often shows infiltration (e.g., amyloid), and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (Option D) is characterized by fibrofatty replacement of the right ventricular myocardium.

q: The skin biopsy image shown is most characteristic of which of the following clinical conditions?
ex: Morphea The image displays histological features characteristic of morphea, also known as localized scleroderma. The key finding is in the dermis, which appears markedly thickened and sclerotic, with dense, eosinophilic collagen bundles that have replaced the normal dermal architecture and subcutaneous fat. There is also a notable loss of skin adnexal structures, such as hair follicles and sweat glands, which become entrapped and atrophied within the fibrotic tissue. The overlying epidermis is often thinned and flattened. This picture reflects the clinical process of excessive collagen deposition leading to hardened, indurated skin plaques. Lichen planus (Option A) is an interface dermatitis with a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate. Lichen nitidus (Option B) shows a claw-and-ball granulomatous infiltrate. Viral myocarditis (Option D) is an inflammation of the heart muscle, not a skin condition.

q: A child presents with pruritic skin lesions along with diarrhea and has been advised to follow a gluten-free diet. What is the most likely underlying etiology of this condition?
ex: Celiac disease Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by ingestion of gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye. It leads to immune-mediated damage of the small intestinal mucosa, particularly the villi, resulting in malabsorption. In children, common symptoms include chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, bloating, weight loss, and nutritional deficiencies. A distinctive extraintestinal manifestation is pruritic skin lesions, known as dermatitis herpetiformis, which occur due to IgA deposition in the dermal papillae. This skin condition is strongly associated with celiac disease and improves with a gluten-free diet. Because gluten triggers the immune response that damages the intestinal lining, the primary treatment is lifelong avoidance of gluten-containing foods. Following a gluten-free diet helps restore the intestinal villi and reduces both gastrointestinal and skin symptoms. The other options are less consistent with the scenario. Whipple's disease is a rare bacterial infection, Crohn’s disease is an inflammatory bowel disease not specifically related to gluten, and dermatitis herpetiformis is actually a cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease rather than the underlying cause. Therefore, the most likely underlying etiology is celiac disease.

q: Which specific antibody is most commonly associated with celiac disease?
o: ANCA (Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies) NODIA 99=== EXAMINATION PAPER 2024
ex: Anti-TTG (Tissue Transglutaminase) The serological diagnosis of Celiac Disease relies on the detection of highly specific autoantibodies. The most sensitive and specific antibody test currently used is the IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-TTG) antibody test. Tissue transglutaminase is the autoantigen in celiac disease; it deamidates gliadin (a component of gluten), which increases its immunogenicity and triggers the autoimmune response. IgA anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA) are also highly specific but the test is more subjective. While anti-gliadin antibodies (AGA) (Option D) were used in the past, they have lower sensitivity and specificity and are no longer recommended for primary diagnosis. ANCA (Option B) is associated with vasculitides like granulomatosis with polyangiitis. ASCA (Option C) is associated with Crohn's disease. Therefore, anti-TTG is the premier antibody marker for celiac disease.

q: In a patient with thalassemia, which viral infection is known to target erythroid progenitor cells and can precipitate aplastic anemia?
ex: Parvovirus B19 Patients with chronic hemolytic anemias, such as thalassemia and sickle cell disease, rely on a hyperactive bone marrow to compensate for the rapid destruction of red blood cells. Parvovirus B19 has a unique tropism for erythroid progenitor cells (the precursors to red blood cells) in the bone marrow. Infection with this virus leads to the lysis of these progenitor cells, causing a temporary cessation of red blood cell production (erythropoiesis). In a person with normal red cell survival, this 7-10 day pause is clinically insignificant. However, in a thalassemia patient with a shortened red cell lifespan, this abrupt halt in production, known as a transient aplastic crisis, leads to a rapid and severe drop in hemoglobin levels, which can be life-threatening. The other viruses listed (CMV, EBV, HCV) can cause bone marrow suppression but are not the classic cause of transient aplastic crisis.

q: A 23-year-old woman with a height of 4 feet is evaluated, and her karyotype is shown in the image below. Which of the following options best explains the underlying etiology of her condition?
ex: Turner syndrome The provided karyotype is 45,X, which is the classic genetic signature for Turner syndrome. This condition is a chromosomal disorder in females characterized by the complete or partial absence of one of the two X chromosomes. The clinical features described, particularly short stature (height of 4 feet), are cardinal signs of Turner syndrome. Other common features include gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries) leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility, a webbed neck, a low posterior hairline, and a broad chest with widely spaced nipples. Cardiac and renal anomalies are also common. Klinefelter's syndrome (Option B) is 47,XXY and affects males. Down syndrome (Option C) is Trisomy 21. Edward's syndrome (Option D) is Trisomy 18. The karyotype is definitive for Turner syndrome.

q: Identify the structure or finding shown in the image and state the disease with which it is associated.
ex: Gaucher's disease The image displays a Gaucher cell, which is the pathognomonic finding in Gaucher's disease. This is a large macrophage (20-100 µm in diameter) whose cytoplasm is filled with undigested glucocerebroside, giving it a characteristic fibrillary or striated appearance often described as wrinkled tissue paper or crumpled silk. Gaucher's disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder, caused by a deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. This leads to the accumulation of glucocerebroside in the lysosomes of macrophages throughout the reticuloendothelial system, particularly in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. This accumulation results in the clinical features of hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and bone disease (pain, fractures). The other options are also lysosomal storage diseases but have different enzymatic defects and stored substrates, and do not feature Gaucher cells.

q: A patient presents with hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal pain, and a markedly elevated white blood cell count exceeding 50,000/mm³. Which underlying gene abnormality is most likely responsible for these findings, and what is the most probable diagnosis?
ex: t(9 :22) The clinical presentation of marked splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, and a very high white blood cell count (leukocytosis) with a spectrum of myeloid precursors is classic for Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML). The molecular hallmark and diagnostic criterion for CML is the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosome 9 and 22, denoted as t(9;22)(q34;q11). This translocation creates a fusion gene called BCR-ABL1 on the shortened chromosome 22 (the Philadelphia chromosome). The protein product of this fusion gene is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives the massive proliferation of granulocytic cells, leading to the clinical and laboratory features of CML. The translocation t(15;17) (Option C) is characteristic of Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL).

q: A male patient diagnosed with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is not responding to oxygen therapy. What role does interleukin-8 (IL-8) play in the pathogenesis of ARDS?
ex: Recruitment of neutrophils Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) is a form of acute, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury characterized by severe hypoxemia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. The pathophysiology involves an uncontrolled inflammatory response within the lungs. A key event is the massive infiltration of neutrophils into the interstitium and alveolar spaces. Interleukin-8 (IL-8), also known as CXCL8, is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant and activator. It is released by activated alveolar macrophages and epithelial cells early in the inflammatory cascade. The high levels of IL-8 in the alveolar fluid of ARDS patients create a strong chemotactic gradient that is primarily responsible for the recruitment of neutrophils from the circulation into the lung tissue. These recruited neutrophils then release proteases, reactive oxygen species, and other inflammatory mediators that damage the alveolar-capillary barrier, leading to protein-rich edema and impaired gas exchange.

q: A patient presents with a renal mass associated with hematuria and flank pain, and a histological image is provided. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Chromophobe Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC) The patient presents with a renal mass, hematuria, and flank pain, which are classic clinical features of renal cell carcinoma (RCC). Histological examination helps differentiate the various subtypes of RCC. In the provided histological image, the tumor cells appear large and polygonal with pale or eosinophilic cytoplasm and well-defined cell borders, giving them a plant-cell–like appearance. The cytoplasm often appears clear or finely granular, and the nuclei are relatively uniform. These features are characteristic of chromophobe renal cell carcinoma. Chromophobe RCC arises from the intercalated cells of the collecting ducts. It typically shows pale cytoplasm, prominent cell membranes, and perinuclear clearing (halo) on microscopy. Compared with other types of RCC, chromophobe carcinoma generally has a better prognosis. The other options have different histological patterns. Clear cell carcinoma shows cells with lipid- and glycogen-rich clear cytoplasm and a delicate vascular network. Papillary RCC shows papillary structures with fibrovascular cores. Bellini duct carcinoma (collecting duct carcinoma) is rare and usually more aggressive. Based on the histological features and clinical presentation, the most likely diagnosis is chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (RCC).

q: Identify the diagnosis from the given image? NODIA 100===
ex: Malakoplakia The histological image is pathognomonic for malakoplakia. This is a rare, chronic inflammatory condition that most commonly affects the urinary tract but can occur in other organs. The key diagnostic feature is the presence of large, eosinophilic histiocytes (macrophages) called von Hansemann cells. Within the cytoplasm of these cells are characteristic laminated, calcified, intracytoplasmic inclusions known as Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. These bodies are thought to represent phagolysosomes containing incompletely digested bacteria (often E. coli) due to a defect in macrophage function. The arrow in the image likely points to one of these targetoid, basophilic Michaelis-Gutmann bodies within a larger macrophage. The condition presents as soft, yellowish plaques or nodules. Tuberculosis (Option A) would show caseating granulomas. Basal cell carcinoma (BCC, Option C) is a skin malignancy with different histology.

q: An adult male presents with a protuberant abdomen, chronic diarrhea, visual disturbances, and neurological symptoms. Laboratory investigations reveal low LDL cholesterol levels, and a peripheral blood smear image is provided. Based on the clinical features and the smear findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Abetalipoproteinemia The key finding in the peripheral smear is the presence of acanthocytes, which are red blood cells with irregular, spiky projections of varying length and width. This finding, combined with the clinical picture of fat malabsorption (diarrhea, protruding abdomen), neurological problems (ataxia, peripheral neuropathy), and visual symptoms (retinitis pigmentosa), along with very low or absent LDL, is diagnostic of Abetalipoproteinemia (also known as Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome). This is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the MTTP gene, which is essential for assembling and secreting apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins (chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL) from enterocytes and hepatocytes. The inability to absorb and transport fats leads to steatorrhea and severe deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which causes the neurological and visual symptoms. The acanthocytosis results from abnormal lipid composition of the red cell membrane.

q: A patient presents with respiratory distress and is diagnosed with panacinar emphysema. Deficiency of which substance is most likely responsible for this condition?
ex: Alpha-1 antitrypsin Emphysema is characterized by the permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by the destruction of their walls. Panacinar (or panlobular) emphysema, which affects the entire acinus uniformly and is most severe in the lower lobes of the lungs, is the classic form associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) deficiency. AAT is a protease inhibitor produced by the liver that circulates in the blood. Its primary function in the lung is to protect the elastic tissue of the alveolar walls from destruction by proteases, particularly neutrophil elastase, which is released by neutrophils during inflammation. In AAT deficiency, this protective shield is absent, leading to unchecked elastase activity and progressive destruction of the lung parenchyma. Centriacinar emphysema, in contrast, is typically associated with smoking. Surfactant (Option B) deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

q: Which of the following statements accurately describes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
o: Flow cytometry is the best investigation
Sucrose lysis test is used for the confirmation
The most common cause of death is heart failure
ex: Flow cytometry is the best investigation Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a rare, acquired (not inherited, so D is incorrect) clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder. It is caused by a somatic mutation in the PIGA gene, which leads to the absence of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins on the surface of blood cells. These missing proteins include CD55 and CD59, which protect cells from complement-mediated destruction. The gold standard and best investigation for diagnosing PNH is flow cytometry. This test can precisely detect and quantify the population of blood cells (red cells, neutrophils, and monocytes) that are deficient in GPI-anchored proteins like CD55 and CD59 on their surface. The sucrose lysis test (Option B) is an older, less specific screening test. The most common cause of death in PNH is thrombosis (venous or arterial), not heart failure (Option C).

q: Based on the dermatology immunofluorescence (IF) image shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Pemphigus vulgaris The image shows a direct immunofluorescence (IF) pattern characteristic of pemphigus vulgaris. In this condition, immunofluorescence demonstrates intercellular deposition of IgG antibodies within the epidermis, producing a net-like or “fish-net/chicken-wire” pattern between keratinocytes. Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disorder caused by autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 (and sometimes desmoglein-1), which are components of desmosomes that help maintain adhesion between epidermal cells. When these antibodies disrupt cell adhesion, acantholysis occurs, leading to intraepidermal blister formation. Clinically, patients present with flaccid bullae and painful erosions, often involving the skin and mucous membranes, especially the oral cavity. A characteristic clinical sign is the Nikolsky sign, where gentle pressure causes the epidermis to separate. The other options show different immunofluorescence patterns:

q: An elderly man presents with clinical features suggestive of multiple myeloma. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates an M spike, and the immunofixation pattern is shown in the image below. Which of the following statements best explains or corresponds to these findings?
o: Multiple myeloma with increased IgG Downloaded from www.pdf.tube 101=== EXAMINATION PAPER 2024
ex: Multiple myeloma with increased IgG The patient's presentation and the M spike on electrophoresis are suggestive of a plasma cell dyscrasia. The immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) is the confirmatory test used to identify the specific type of monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) being produced. In the provided IFE gel, a distinct, dense band is seen in two specific lanes : the lane corresponding to the IgG heavy chain and the lane corresponding to the kappa (κ) light chain. This result indicates that the malignant plasma cells are producing a monoclonal protein composed of an IgG heavy chain and a kappa light chain. Therefore, the diagnosis is IgG kappa Multiple Myeloma. This is the most common type of multiple myeloma. Waldenström macroglobulinemia (Option D) is characterized by an IgM monoclonal protein (Option A). An IgA M-protein (Option C) would show a band in the IgA lane.

q: A patient presents with pulmonary hemorrhage and tests positive for p-ANCA, with involvement of medium-sized blood vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Microscopic polyangiitis This question describes a case of ANCA-associated vasculitis. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is a necrotizing vasculitis that primarily affects small vessels (capillaries, venules, arterioles), though medium-sized vessels can be involved. Its classic presentation involves necrotizing glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis, which manifests as pulmonary hemorrhage. A key laboratory finding in MPA is the presence of perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (P-ANCA), which are typically directed against the antigen myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA). Churg-Strauss syndrome (EGPA, Option A) also is often P-ANCA positive but is distinguished by a history of asthma and prominent eosinophilia. Wegener's granulomatosis (GPA, Option C) is characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract and is strongly associated with C-ANCA (PR3-ANCA). Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN, Option D) affects medium-sized vessels but is ANCA-negative and typically spares the lungs.

q: Which of the following findings is most commonly seen on laboratory investigations in a patient with iron deficiency anemia (IDA)?
ex: Decreased transferrin saturation Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by the depletion of the body's iron stores. This leads to a distinct pattern on iron studies. Serum ferritin is a measure of stored iron, so in IDA, it is the first marker to fall and will be decreased, not increased (Option A is incorrect). Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is an indirect measure of transferrin, the protein that transports iron. The liver increases transferrin production in an attempt to capture more iron, so TIBC is increased, not normal (Option D is incorrect). Serum iron measures the amount of iron circulating in the blood, which will be low in IDA (Option C is incorrect). Transferrin saturation is the ratio of serum iron to TIBC (Serum Iron / TIBC × 100%). Since serum iron is low and TIBC is high, the resulting saturation percentage is significantly decreased, typically to less than 15%. This is a hallmark of IDA.

q: An adult woman presents with pallor and fatigue, and laboratory investigations reveal low hemoglobin, reduced serum iron, low ferritin levels, decreased transferrin saturation, and increased total iron-binding capacity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) The pattern of laboratory results provided is the classic and definitive profile for Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). The low hemoglobin confirms anemia. The low serum ferritin indicates that the body's iron stores are depleted. The low serum iron shows there is insufficient iron in circulation. The increased Total Iron-Binding Capacity (TIBC) reflects the liver's compensatory response of producing more transferrin protein to try and bind more iron from the diet. Finally, the low transferrin saturation (the percentage of transferrin that is actually carrying iron) is a direct consequence of low iron and high TIBC. In contrast, Anemia of Chronic Disease (Option B) typically presents with low serum iron but normal or increased ferritin (as it's an acute phase reactant) and a low TIBC. Hemolytic anemia (Option C) involves red cell destruction, and thalassemia (Option D) is a disorder of globin chain synthesis; neither shows this iron study pattern.

q: Which of the following findings or complications is not typically associated with resection of the ileum?
ex: Microcytic hypochromic anemia The terminal ileum is the primary site for absorption of vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) and bile salts. When the ileum is resected, absorption of vitamin B₁₂ is impaired, which can lead to vitamin B₁₂ deficiency. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency results in megaloblastic anemia, characterized by macrocytic red blood cells and impaired DNA synthesis. One important microscopic feature of this condition is nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony, where the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm in developing blood cells. Therefore, nuclear cytological asynchrony is associated with ileal resection. Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency can also cause neurological manifestations, such as peripheral neuropathy, paresthesia, ataxia, and degeneration of the spinal cord (subacute combined degeneration). In severe cases, it may lead to cognitive impairment or reversible dementia, which can improve after vitamin B₁₂ supplementation. In contrast, microcytic hypochromic anemia is usually caused by iron deficiency. Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, not the ileum. Therefore, ileal resection does not typically lead to iron deficiency anemia. Hence, the finding not associated with ileal resection is microcytic hypochromic anemia, making Option (A) correct.

q: A child presents with recurrent infections, and imaging of the mediastinum shows absence of the thymus. Further laboratory evaluation reveals low levels of adenosine deaminase (ADA). What is the most likely diagnosis?
ex: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) The combination of an absent thymus (or thymic shadow on X-ray) and recurrent severe infections points towards a profound T-cell immunodeficiency. While an absent thymus is the hallmark of DiGeorge syndrome (Option B), the laboratory finding of low adenosine deaminase (ADA) levels is specific for a particular autosomal recessive form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID). ADA deficiency accounts for about 15% of SCID cases. The ADA enzyme is crucial for purine metabolism. Its absence leads to the accumulation of toxic metabolites (deoxyadenosine and dATP), which are particularly toxic to developing lymphocytes. This results in a severe impairment of both T-cell and B-cell function, leading to the combined immunodeficiency. Although both conditions can have an absent thymus on imaging, the specific enzyme deficiency (low ADA) definitively points to SCID as the diagnosis.

q: A patient presents with episodic headaches, palpitations, and hypertension, and urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) testing is positive. A biopsy image is provided. Based on the clinical features and histopathological findings, which of the following statements is correct?
ex: Associated with MEN 2A The clinical triad of episodic headaches, palpitations, and sweating, along with hypertension and elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), is classic for a pheochromocytoma, a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla. The histology shows the characteristic Zellballen pattern (nests of chief cells). While most pheochromocytomas are sporadic, a significant portion (around 25-30%) are hereditary. They are a key feature of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2A (MEN 2A) and 2B. MEN 2A is an autosomal dominant syndrome (caused by RET proto-oncogene mutations) characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism. Regarding the other options : approximately 10% are malignant (A is incorrect), they can occur in children but are more common in adults (B is incorrect), and about 10% are bilateral (more common in hereditary cases) (C is incorrect). The association with MEN 2A is a well-established and important clinical fact.

q: An adult tall male presents with an increased arm span, pectus excavatum, and associated cardiac abnormalities. Deficiency or defect of which protein is most likely responsible for these features?
ex: Fibrillin This clinical presentation is classic for Marfan syndrome. It is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder characterized by skeletal abnormalities (tall stature, long limbs and fingers - arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum or carinatum, scoliosis), ocular problems (ectopia lentis - lens dislocation), and cardiovascular manifestations (aortic root aneurysm and dissection, mitral valve prolapse). Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in the FBN1 gene, which codes for the protein fibrillin-1. Fibrillin-1 is a major component of extracellular microfibrils, which provide structural support to connective tissues throughout the body, particularly in the aorta, ligaments, and the ciliary zonules of the eye. Defective fibrillin-1 leads to weakened connective tissue, explaining the multisystemic features of the disease. Elastin (Option B) mutations cause other conditions like cutis laxa.

q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a gradually progressive, painless swelling on the left side of her neck that has been present for the past two months. She also complains of low- grade fever, night sweats, and unintentional NODIA 102=== weight loss during this period. On physical examination, there is a firm, non-tender, and immobile mass in the left cervical region, along with multiple smaller lymph nodes palpable in the supraclavicular area. A chest X-ray reveals widening of the mediastinum. Lymph node biopsy demonstrates the presence of Reed– Sternberg cells, confirming the diagnosis. Based on these clinical, radiological, and histopathological findings, what is the most appropriate management for this patient?
o: NHL with a highly aggressive chemotherapy regimen
Hodgkin Lymphoma with the ABVD regimen
Hodgkin Lymphoma with surgical excision only
ex: Hodgkin Lymphoma with the ABVD regimen The patient's presentation with painless lymphadenopathy, constitutional B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), and the definitive histological finding of Reed-Sternberg cells is diagnostic of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma. Surgical excision alone (Option D) is not curative as the disease is often systemic. Hodgkin lymphoma is highly sensitive to chemotherapy and radiation. This regimen has high cure rates and has been the gold standard for decades. q: A patient who underwent surgery three years ago now presents with the condition shown in the image and complains of decreased vision. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) or arsenic trioxide helps overcome the differentiation block, allowing the leukemic promyelocytes to mature into normal cells.
